efet_body:

Kebs warns against misuse of quality mark on miraa juices
Kebs says it has revoked permits in identified cases and warns manufacturers and traders against falsely claiming approval for khat-infused beverages.
by
EMMANUEL WANJALA
Share
Audio By Vocalize
Miraa for sale at a market /FILE
The Kenya Bureau of Standards has warned manufacturers and traders against displaying its Standardization Mark of quality on khat-infused beverages, saying the products are not covered by its certification.
In a notice dated October 16, Kebs said it has established that some manufacturers certified to produce fruit juices and fruit drinks were using permits issued for those products to market beverages infused with khat.
The regulator said the practice misrepresented the certification status of the beverages and could attract enforcement action under the Standards Act, Cap 496.
“Kebs wishes to clarify that certification permits are valid only for the products covered by the approved scope of certification and do not extend to khat-infused beverages or any other products outside that scope,” the notice stated.
The bureau emphasised that certification for fruit juices and fruit drinks did not automatically authorise manufacturers to use the same permits for products containing khat.
“Kebs has therefore not issued Standardization Mark permits for any khat-infused beverages,” the statement added.
The notice was issued under the authority of Kebs director general Esther Ngari, who said the bureau had taken action against identified cases of non-compliance and would continue monitoring the market.
“Kebs has revoked certification permits in identified cases of non-compliance and will continue to undertake market surveillance and take appropriate action against manufacturers and traders found misusing the Standardization Mark,” the statement said.
Khat, popularly known as miraa, muguka or jaba, is a recognised cash crop legally grown, traded and consumed in Kenya.
However, its stimulant properties cathinone and cathine have also placed it under public health scrutiny, particularly over concerns about dependence and substance use disorders.
The National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse (Nacada) classifies khat alongside alcohol and tobacco as a substance that can contribute to dependence and substance use disorders.
Kebs explained that the presence of the naturally occurring stimulant compounds in the plant is central to concerns about its effects on users.
“Manufacturers and traders are therefore cautioned against displaying the KEBS Standardization Mark or making claims of KEBS certification on khat-infused beverages,” the notice stated.
Consumers were also warned that any representation that such beverages had been certified by Kebs was misleading.
The bureau urged members of the public to verify the certification status of products through its official channels, including SMS 20023, and report suspected misuse of the Standardization Mark through its toll-free number, 1545.
Kebs said the measures were intended to protect consumers, preserve the integrity of its certification system and ensure compliance with applicable Kenya Standards and regulatory requirements.

efet_title: KEBS warns against substandard products as Kenya embraces clean energy - The Star, Kenya
efet_body:
ADVERTISEMENT

14 October 2026 - 18:56
KEBS warns against substandard products as Kenya embraces clean energy
KEBS says stronger quality checks on solar panels, batteries and electrical appliances are needed to protect consumers and support affordable clean energy
by
PERPETUA ETYANG
Share
Audio By Vocalize
KEBS Director General Esther Ngari at the World Standards Day celebrations in Nairobi on October 14, 2026 / HANDOUT
The Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) has called for stronger enforcement of quality standards in the energy sector, warning that substandard products could undermine Kenya’s transition to affordable and clean energy.
KEBS Director General Esther Ngari said standards were essential to ensuring that solar panels, batteries and electrical appliances met safety, quality and efficiency requirements as households and businesses increasingly adopted modern energy technologies.
Speaking on Wednesday during the World Standards Day celebrations in Nairobi, Ngari said inefficient equipment could increase operating costs for households and businesses, undermining efforts to make energy affordable.
She added that standards provide agreed requirements for assessing product safety, quality, performance and efficiency, enabling consumers to make informed choices.
“A solar panel that fails prematurely, a battery that does not deliver the expected performance, or an electrical appliance that presents a safety risk can turn an investment in progress into a source of loss or disappointment,” Ngari said.
Ngari said KEBS would continue working with regulators, manufacturers, importers and research institutions to ensure standards responded to emerging technologies and the country's economic needs.
“Our responsibility is therefore both protective and developmental. We must help ensure that products in the market meet applicable requirements while enabling responsible businesses to demonstrate quality and build consumer confidence,” she said.
She cited collaboration between KEBS and the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) on fuel quality as an example of how institutions with complementary mandates could support consumer protection, fair trade and environmental objectives.
The celebrations were held under the theme
Shared Vision for a Better World
, focusing on Sustainable Development Goal Seven, which seeks to ensure access to affordable and clean energy.
Speaking at the event, former president of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and former KenGen managing director Eddy Njoroge said standards would be critical to expanding access to reliable, affordable and clean energy across Africa.
Njoroge, who chairs the Electricity Sector Association of Kenya, cited figures from the 2026 edition of
Tracking SDG 7
, which show that about 655 million people worldwide still lack access to electricity, including more than 560 million in sub-Saharan Africa.
He said around two billion people globally continued to rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking.
He said the success of energy access initiatives should be measured by their impact on people's lives rather than solely by the number of power plants built or electricity connections made.
“For Africa, then, clean and affordable energy is not simply an environmental ambition. It is a development imperative. Our farms, factories, hospitals, schools, businesses and communications networks all depend on energy. Without it, opportunity narrows,” Njoroge said.
He said reliable energy enabled hospitals to refrigerate vaccines, children to study after sunset, farmers to irrigate their land and manufacturers to operate machinery at competitive costs.
Njoroge urged African countries to strengthen their participation in developing international standards, saying the continent's energy challenges required solutions informed by local expertise and experience.
He cited KEBS' role as the secretariat of ISO Technical Committee 285, which develops standards for clean cookstoves and clean cooking solutions, as an example of Kenya's contribution to global standardisation.
Established in 2013, the committee's work covers the testing and assessment of stove safety, emissions, efficiency and performance. ISO currently lists seven published standards under the committee.
“This means a Kenyan voice is helping set the global yardstick for what ‘clean’ really means in a kitchen. It means Kenyan expertise is helping to shape how the world judges cleaner and safer cooking technology. Africa is not simply receiving standards; it is helping write them,” he said.
Njoroge said millions of households in Kenya still cooked using firewood and charcoal, exposing families, particularly women and children, to harmful smoke. He said access to modern energy should therefore include cleaner cooking solutions and not be limited to electricity connections.

efet_body:
Police seize 114 crates of suspected illicit alcohol in Kirinyaga
By
Johnson Muriithi
October 19, 2026 08:33 (EAT)
Add as a Preferred
Source on Google
Follow us
Follow on Whatsapp
Follow on Google
Follow on Twitter
An illustration of Illicit brew, which has claimed more than 17 lives in Kirinyaga County.
Audio By Vocalize
Police in Kirinyaga County have seized 114 crates of suspected illicit alcohol in Mwea East Sub-County following a tip-off about a lorry transporting the consignment to a local bar depot.
Mwea East Sub-County Police Commander Henry Gitonga said officers intercepted the consignment at Murubara, where they recovered 114 crates of Diamond Ice and 200 empty crates.
Gitonga said the officers subsequently raided another bar dealing in wines and spirits, seizing four cartons of People Vodka and nine other cartons containing People Gin and lemonades.
Police also seized 11 cartons of suspected illicit alcohol in the Ngurubani area during the operation.
The seized products have been detained at Wang’uru Police Station as exhibits pending testing by the Government Chemist, the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) and the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) to establish their authenticity.
Gitonga noted that although the consignment bore KRA and KEBS stamps, authorities would subject the products to further examination to determine whether they met the required standards.
The seizure has sparked renewed concern among residents over the circulation of suspected illicit alcohol in the region, with questions being raised about its source and distribution networks.
Some residents have called on the government to restrict the sale of ethanol, which they blame for contributing to the proliferation of illicit alcoholic drinks.
Others, however, argue that bar owners also depend on suppliers and that enforcement efforts should target the entire distribution chain, including those manufacturing and transporting the products.
Residents expressed concern over the growing presence of unfamiliar beer brands and other alcoholic drinks in the market, warning that some could pose serious health risks to consumers, particularly young people.
“They should allow Makabo and Muratina to be sold in local bars,” said resident Mugo Gikombe, referring to traditional alcoholic drinks.
Residents also urged security agencies to intensify surveillance and establish roadblocks along key routes to curb the transportation and distribution of suspected illicit alcohol into the area.
John Maina said some of the products were allegedly being transported from other counties, while others were suspected to be manufactured locally.
“Some of those fake brands are being brought here from other counties, while others are made locally by our people in their local bars. Something needs to be done before our youths are finished,” Maina said.
The residents called for coordinated action by security agencies and regulatory authorities to identify the suppliers, verify the safety and authenticity of alcoholic products on the market, and hold those responsible for distributing illicit drinks accountable.
The seized consignment remains at Wang’uru Police Station as investigations and laboratory tests are awaited.
